Do not give a dose.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"LactMed\u2019s amoxicillin entry reports:\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n- In milk samples from **6 women**, average amoxicillin concentrations were **0.69 mg/L** (range **0.46\u20130.88 mg/L**) at 4 hours and **0.81 mg/L** (range **0.39\u20131.3 mg/L**) at 5 hours after administration. These are **milk concentrations**, not infant-level measurements. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)\\n- For **infant levels**, LactMed states that relevant published information was **not found as of the revision date**. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\n### Observed infant symptoms\\n- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, **3 infants had diarrhea**; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that group. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)\\n- In a prospective study of **40 infants exposed through breast milk**, **2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash**. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)\\n- In a study comparing amoxicillin-exposed infants with macrolide-exposed infants, reported reactions among the amoxicillin-exposed infants occurred in **8.3%** and included **rash and somnolence**. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)\\n- One case involved recurrent **generalized urticaria** after breastfeeding. The mother was receiving **amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin**, so the responsible drug could not be determined; LactMed reported that the combination product was considered the more likely cause. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)\\n- Another report described **mild diarrhea** in an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin along with acetaminophen plus codeine; the relationship was rated possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)\\n- In a study of 25 mothers and infants older than 4 weeks, **no infant adverse effects were reported**. This does not establish that adverse effects never occur. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)\\n\\n### Advice to monitor\\nThe retrieved LactMed text does **not** provide a separate recommendation that parents monitor for particular symptoms. It says that one study had mothers monitor for tongue changes, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change, and jaundice; that was the study\u2019s data collection, not necessarily LactMed advice. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\n### Uncertainty\\nLactMed states that rash and disruption of gastrointestinal flora, resulting in diarrhea or thrush, have been reported but **\u201chave not been adequately evaluated.\u201d** The record includes different study methods, comparison groups, co-exposures, and reports involving combination products, so the findings do not establish that amoxicillin caused every reported symptom. Infant-level exposure information was missing in the retrieved record. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed copy was revised **2026-06-15** and came from an official package published **2026-10-22**; the MCP identifies this as a bounded extract rather than a complete record. [S3](https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/litarch/file_list.csv)[S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\nThe MCP also notes that stopping or changing a medication can carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThis LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.\\nHuman clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.\\nStopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.\\n\\nInformational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. request.question: What does LactMed report about amoxicillin in breastfed babies? Separate observed symptoms from advice to monitor, and explain uncertainty. Do not give a dose.

response.answer:
LactMed’s amoxicillin entry reports:

### Measured exposure
- In milk samples from **6 women**, average amoxicillin concentrations were **0.69 mg/L** (range **0.46–0.88 mg/L**) at 4 hours and **0.81 mg/L** (range **0.39–1.3 mg/L**) at 5 hours after administration. These are **milk concentrations**, not infant-level measurements. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)
- For **infant levels**, LactMed states that relevant published information was **not found as of the revision date**. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

### Observed infant symptoms
- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, **3 infants had diarrhea**; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that group. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)
- In a prospective study of **40 infants exposed through breast milk**, **2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash**. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)
- In a study comparing amoxicillin-exposed infants with macrolide-exposed infants, reported reactions among the amoxicillin-exposed infants occurred in **8.3%** and included **rash and somnolence**. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)
- One case involved recurrent **generalized urticaria** after breastfeeding. The mother was receiving **amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin**, so the responsible drug could not be determined; LactMed reported that the combination product was considered the more likely cause. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)
- Another report described **mild diarrhea** in an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin along with acetaminophen plus codeine; the relationship was rated possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)
- In a study of 25 mothers and infants older than 4 weeks, **no infant adverse effects were reported**. This does not establish that adverse effects never occur. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)

### Advice to monitor
The retrieved LactMed text does **not** provide a separate recommendation that parents monitor for particular symptoms. It says that one study had mothers monitor for tongue changes, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change, and jaundice; that was the study’s data collection, not necessarily LactMed advice. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

### Uncertainty
LactMed states that rash and disruption of gastrointestinal flora, resulting in diarrhea or thrush, have been reported but **“have not been adequately evaluated.”** The record includes different study methods, comparison groups, co-exposures, and reports involving combination products, so the findings do not establish that amoxicillin caused every reported symptom. Infant-level exposure information was missing in the retrieved record. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

The retrieved LactMed copy was revised **2026-06-15** and came from an official package published **2026-10-22**; the MCP identifies this as a bounded extract rather than a complete record. [S3](https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/litarch/file_list.csv)[S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

The MCP also notes that stopping or changing a medication can carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.

request.question: For sumatriptan during breastfeeding, what was measured in milk and what was actually observed in infants? If those are different kinds of evidence, explain that. No personal medication advice.

response.answer:
### Measured exposure

LactMed reports sumatriptan concentrations measured in **breastmilk**:

- In five breastfeeding women, peak milk concentration averaged **87.2 mcg/L** (range **62–113 mcg/L**), measured about **2.5 hours** after administration.
- In a separate group of seven women, peak milk concentration averaged **59.3 mcg/L** (range **24.6–112.8 mcg/L**), occurring **2–4 hours** after administration. The average milk concentration was **23.2 mcg/L** (range **7.7–50.6 mcg/L**).
- **Infant levels:** Relevant published information was **not found as of the LactMed revision date**. Thus, the retrieved record reports milk concentrations, but not measured concentrations in an infant specimen. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/) [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8866921/) [S2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33730376/)

### What was observed in infants

LactMed describes manufacturer correspondence involving **three women** who used sumatriptan during breastfeeding; none reported adverse effects in their infants. The infants’ drug levels were not reported, and the exposure details were unspecified. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

These are different types of evidence: milk concentrations measure **drug exposure in breastmilk**, whereas the three-infant account reports **reported clinical observations**. The infant observation does not establish infant drug concentrations, and the milk measurements do not by themselves establish an infant clinical outcome.

The LactMed record was revised **December 15, 2025**. The returned material is a bounded extract, so absence of additional findings from it is not evidence of safety. The MCP lookup also notes that stopping or changing a medication can carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.

request.question: Compare metformin label warnings for the adult taking it with findings in breastfed infants. Identify which source says what, and disclose missing sections. Don't give any doses.

response.answer:
## Metformin: adult label warnings compared with breastfed-infant findings

### Adult medicine-taker label

The retrieved label is for **METFORMIN HCL TABLET [QPHARMA, INC.]**. The exact product/formulation was not confirmed. Its **Warnings** section identifies lactic acidosis as a rare, serious complication associated with metformin accumulation and discusses increased risk in renal dysfunction and conditions involving hypoxemia, hypoperfusion, dehydration, sepsis, hepatic disease, or heart failure. The retrieved warning text is truncated. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

The label’s adult adverse-reactions section reports gastrointestinal reactions—including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, and abdominal discomfort—as well as other reported reactions, including hypoglycemia. These findings come from adult patients with type 2 diabetes and are not infant outcomes. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

The label’s **lactation** section says animal studies found metformin in milk, that comparable studies had not been conducted in nursing mothers, and that potential infant hypoglycemia was a concern. This is a label warning, not an observed infant outcome. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

### Breastfed-infant evidence

LactMed reports measured exposure and observed outcomes separately. Its population is lactating women and breastfed infants; some infant ages, extent of nursing, and postpartum timing were unspecified. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

#### Measured exposure

Reported **milk metformin concentrations** included:

- **270 mcg/L** averaged over 24 hours in six women.
- About **380 mcg/L** in one woman approximately 4–5 hours after administration.
- **130 and 270 mcg/L** in two women measured over 72 hours.
- **130–270 mcg/L** in three women.
- An average of **410 mcg/L** in women studied 4–17 days postpartum.

LactMed also reports **infant serum** measurements: in four infants, two results were below **10 mcg/L**, while two were **50 and 80 mcg/L**; in two other measured infants, levels were below **5 mcg/L**. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)  
The underlying transfer studies are cited by LactMed at [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12436333/), [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12545145/), [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15384618/), and [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15932841/).

#### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reports that:

- Seven infants aged 5–25 months were judged healthy, with expected growth and development; two had normal Denver developmental screening results. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12436333/)
- Three infants had no detectable adverse effects attributed to metformin. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15384618/)
- In three breastfed infants aged 10–11 days postpartum, none had low blood glucose, and their mothers reported no adverse reactions. [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15932841/)
- In a prospective study of 111 infants—61 predominantly breastfed and 50 formula-fed—no differences were found at 3 or 6 months in height, weight, motor-social development, or illness rates. The reported study population included infants of women treated with metformin for polycystic ovary syndrome; the retrieved LactMed extract does not establish a complete study count. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16737874/)

These observations do not establish that every possible label concern was absent, and the label warning should not be converted into an infant outcome.

### Comparison

| Topic | Adult label says | Breastfeeding sources report |
|---|---|---|
| Serious metabolic warning | Lactic acidosis is a serious complication associated with metformin accumulation in the medicine-taker population. | No lactic-acidosis outcome was reported in the retrieved infant findings. Silence in these extracts is not proof that it cannot occur. |
| Hypoglycemia | Hypoglycemia appears among reported adult adverse reactions; the lactation section raises potential infant hypoglycemia as a concern. | One reported group of three infants had no low blood glucose; this is an observed result from that group, not a general conclusion. |
| Gastrointestinal effects | Adult adverse reactions include diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, and abdominal discomfort. | The retrieved infant-outcome passages do not report these gastrointestinal effects in infants. |
| Drug exposure | The warning discusses maternal accumulation. | LactMed reports measured milk concentrations and infant serum concentrations separately from clinical outcomes. |

### Missing sections and limitations

- The retrieved label omitted **`warnings_and_precautions`** and **`boxed_warning`**; the **Warnings** text was truncated. Their absence in this extract is not proof that the corresponding material is absent from the full labeling. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)
- The LactMed extract returned all four expected sections and was not marked truncated, but its study count was not established in the retrieved data, and several population or timing details were unspecified. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)
- The LactMed record is a saved copy of an NLM package; the returned record was revised August 15, 2026, and the package was published October 22, 2026. [S2](https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/litarch/file_list.csv)

request.question: Search FDA recall records for naproxen. The fictional bottle lot is NOTREAL-77. If the lot is not found, can the lookup establish that the bottle was unaffected? Explain what still needs verification.

### Still requiring verification

Verify the bottle’s exact:

- formulation and product name;
- manufacturer or repackager;
- NDC or other product identifier;
- lot number, including any prefixes, suffixes, spaces, or transcription differences;
- expiration date; and
- match against the applicable official recall notice, including any lot range or all-lot language.

The MCP-generated lookup guidance also notes that FDA enforcement records may lag announcements and may not contain all consumer instructions. Confirm the bottle-specific status with the manufacturer, dispensing pharmacy, or pharmacist, using the official FDA recall page as a reference. The lookup’s limitations state that candidate product-name matches are not bottle-level clearance, and that a missing lot match, different lot, or terminated recall does not prove the product safe. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/enforcement.json?search=product_description%3A%22naproxen%22&sort=report_date%3Adesc&limit=20)

### Still requiring verification

Verify the bottle’s exact:

- formulation and product name;
- manufacturer or repackager;
- NDC or other product identifier;
- lot number, including any prefixes, suffixes, spaces, or transcription differences;
- expiration date; and
- match against the applicable official recall notice, including any lot range or all-lot language.

The MCP-generated lookup guidance also notes that FDA enforcement records may lag announcements and may not contain all consumer instructions. Confirm the bottle-specific status with the manufacturer, dispensing pharmacy, or pharmacist, using the official FDA recall page as a reference. [S14](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/drug-recalls)

request.question: Is there an FDA-listed pregnancy exposure registry covering topiramate? Give the listing and registry contact or enrollment link if returned, and distinguish finding a registry from being eligible to enroll.

response.answer:
Yes. The FDA directory lists **The North American Antiepileptic Drug in Pregnancy Registry** for **Topamax, Trokendi XR, and Qudexy XR (topiramate)**, for epilepsy, mood disorder, and migraine headaches. Its status is listed as **Ongoing**. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

- **Enrollment/contact:** https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/ [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)
- **Telephone:** 1-888-233-2334 [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

This listing does **not** establish individual eligibility or current site availability. The study team must confirm both directly. The FDA directory also states that it lists but does not operate or endorse the registries, and that the list is not comprehensive. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

request.question: Find up to two recruiting ADHD studies involving children in the United States. Include exact study links, overall and site status if present, update dates, contacts and qualification limits. Do not decide whether a child qualifies.

response.answer:
## Recruiting ADHD studies involving children in the United States

Two records were returned. The registry’s **source population field is not established for either study**; the age ranges below come from the registry age fields and eligibility text. These are potential matches, not confirmed eligibility. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

### 1. Virtual-reality interventions for ADHD — NCT05608434

**Exact study link:** [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05608434)  
**Study type:** Interventional  
**Source population:** Not established in the returned record  
**Overall status:** **RECRUITING**  
**Last update posted:** **November 12, 2026**  
**Results:** No results posted.

**Qualification limits stated in the registry:**

- Age **8–16 years**; the pilot phase specifies **10–16 years**.
- ADHD diagnosis, or prominent impairing inattention symptoms in at least two settings that do not meet the stated diagnostic threshold.
- Parent consent and child assent.
- Main-trial screening requires the listed ADHD symptom-score threshold.
- Availability for in-person visits at the NIH Clinical Center in Bethesda.
- Other exclusions include specified cognitive, neurological, visual, psychiatric, medical, prior-intervention, and study-procedure circumstances.
- The registry contains phase-specific medication-related criteria; the study team must explain how those criteria apply.

**Site status:**

- National Institutes of Health Clinical Center, Bethesda, Maryland — **RECRUITING**

**Contacts:**

- Saadia A. Choudhury — (301) 437-0489 — saadia.choudhury@nih.gov
- Daniel S. Pine, M.D. — (301) 594-1318 — daniel.pine@nih.gov
- NIH Office of Patient Recruitment — 800-411-1222 — ccopr@nih.gov

### 2. SPN-812 (viloxazine extended-release) in preschool-age children with ADHD — NCT04781140

**Exact study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04781140)  
**Study type:** Interventional  
**Source population:** Not established in the returned record  
**Overall status:** **RECRUITING**  
**Last update posted:** **October 5, 2026**  
**Results:** No results posted.

**Qualification limits stated in the registry:**

- Age **4 years 0 months through 5 years 9 months**.
- Primary ADHD diagnosis confirmed using the listed diagnostic interview.
- Minimum ADHD symptom-score and severity-score thresholds at screening and baseline.
- The listed requirements concerning behavioral treatment, structured group activity, parent or guardian consent, and other study procedures.
- Exclusions include specified psychiatric, neurological, systemic, cardiovascular, dietary/swallowing, investigational-drug, medication, and suicidality-related criteria.

**Site statuses returned:**

- **RECRUITING:** Saraland, Alabama; Little Rock, Arkansas; Anaheim, Imperial, and Long Beach, California; Centennial, Colorado; Coral Gables, Jacksonville, Miami, Orange City, Orlando, and Tamarac, Florida.
- **WITHDRAWN:** Fayetteville, Arkansas; Encino and Newport Beach, California; Clermont, Florida.
- **TERMINATED:** Garden Grove, California; Gainesville and Lakeland, Florida.

The returned site list is truncated.

**Central contact:**

- Olivia Elbaum — 301-838-2500 — clinicaltrials@supernus.com

**Returned recruiting-site contacts include:**

- Saraland, Alabama — 251-341-7021 — info@thecenterforclinicaltrials.com
- Little Rock, Arkansas — 501-553-9987 — info@preferredresearchpartners.com
- Anaheim, California — 714-999-6688 — contact@arctrials.com
- Imperial, California — 760-545-0123 — svrcinfo@sunvalleyb.com
- Long Beach, California — 562-548-8500 — Research@asclepes.com
- Centennial, Colorado — 303-771-9000 or 303-773-9000 — verosinfo@veroshealth.com
- Coral Gables, Florida — 305-613-7761
- Jacksonville, Florida — 904-281-5757
- Miami, Florida — 305-515-9006 — info@avantisclinicalresearch.com
- Orange City, Florida — 386-775-7627
- Orlando, Florida — 407-425-5100 — orlinfo@cnshealthcare.com; 407-423-7149, extension 166 or 165 — kkenworthyapg@gmail.com
- Tamarac, Florida — 786-375-6210 — info@dhnrc.com

**Search limitations:** This was a bounded search of the first 20 API matches using literal ADHD terms and the child filter; synonyms may have been missed. Overall recruiting status does not establish that every listed site is currently enrolling. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

request.question: Are any recruiting pediatric epilepsy studies returned for Canada? Show up to two with study links and contacts, or clearly explain if the search found none. Do not substitute completed studies.

response.answer:
One indirect/unverified recruiting match was returned; no directly confirmed pediatric epilepsy study was established by this bounded search. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=pediatric+epilepsy+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=Canada)

### Real World Evidence on the Use of Medical Cannabis in Pediatrics
- **Status:** RECRUITING
- **Study type:** OBSERVATIONAL
- **Population:** Children ages 3–17 years; the registry summary describes children with authorizations for medical cannabis across Canada. The source population for pediatric epilepsy specifically is not established.
- **Epilepsy relevance:** “Epilepsy” appears in the conditions field, but the search marked the match **indirect_or_unverified** and did not confirm clinical suitability for epilepsy.
- **Canada site:** U Manitoba, Winnipeg, Manitoba — **RECRUITING**
- **Study link:** https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910 [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910)
- **Contact:** Lauren E. Kelly, PhD — lauren.kelly@umanitoba.ca; +1 204-272-3149

The search returned one record and did not substitute completed studies. It screened only the first 20 API matches and used literal topic words; synonyms may have been missed. Overall registry recruitment does not establish that every location is recruiting. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability; this lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=pediatric+epilepsy+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=Canada)

request.question: Where is the official FDA page a parent can use to report a possible medication problem? Does a report by itself show that the medicine caused the problem? Please don't ask me for identifying information or file anything.

response.answer:
The official FDA page is **FDA MedWatch: Safety Information and Adverse Event Reporting Program**: [S3](https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program)

A report by itself does **not** establish that the medicine caused the problem. The retrieved FDA resource describes it as reporting a suspected medicine problem and states that a report does not establish causation. No report was filed.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find a PubMed paper about levetiracetam while breastfeeding, retrieve its abstract, and summarize only the study design, population and findings actually available. Distinguish drug exposure from infant outcomes.

response.answer:
**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?*  
**PMID:** 34131926 — [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Study design
The abstract does not state a formal design label. It reports that breastfeeding women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam completed a questionnaire. Researchers measured levetiracetam concentrations in serial breast-milk samples collected from before administration through 12 hours afterward, and in one pre-dose maternal-serum sample. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Population
The study included 20 breastfeeding women and 21 infants; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. Infant ages, gestational ages, and prematurity status were not provided in the abstract. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Drug exposure
The abstract reports:

- A trough breast-milk/maternal-serum levetiracetam ratio of **0.98 ± 0.20**.
- Relative infant exposure estimates of **13.8 ± 3.1%** among fully breastfed infants and **6.9 ± 1.6%** among partially breastfed infants.
- Correlations among maternal levetiracetam exposure, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations, and breast-milk AUC values. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Infant outcomes
- Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants.
- The abstract states that the somnolence resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding.
- The abstract states that all infants gained weight according to age.
- Longer-term infant outcomes were not reported in the abstract. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

The abstract states that further studies are needed to assess short- and long-term safety. This study’s reported exposure measurements and outcomes do not determine an individual medication plan. The PubMed abstract was successfully retrieved; this was a single-record lookup, not a complete literature review.

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

{"answer": "**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?*  
**PMID:** 34131926 — [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Study design
The abstract does not state a formal design label. It reports that breastfeeding women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam completed a questionnaire. Researchers measured levetiracetam concentrations in serial breast-milk samples collected from before administration through 12 hours afterward, and in one pre-dose maternal-serum sample. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Population
The study included 20 breastfeeding women and 21 infants; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. Infant ages, gestational ages, and prematurity status were not provided in the abstract. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Drug exposure
The abstract reports:

- A trough breast-milk/maternal-serum levetiracetam ratio of **0.98 ± 0.20**.
- Relative infant exposure estimates of **13.8 ± 3.1%** among fully breastfed infants and **6.9 ± 1.6%** among partially breastfed infants.
- Correlations among maternal levetiracetam exposure, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations, and breast-milk AUC values. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Infant outcomes
- Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants.
- The abstract states that the somnolence resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding.
- The abstract states that all infants gained weight according to age.
- Longer-term infant outcomes were not reported in the abstract. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

The abstract states that further studies are needed to assess short- and long-term safety. This study’s reported exposure measurements and outcomes do not determine an individual medication plan. The PubMed abstract was successfully retrieved; this was a single-record lookup, not a complete literature review.

Application limits:

request.question: What can infant adverse-event reports involving acetaminophen tell a researcher, and what can they not establish about how often side effects occur or whether the medicine caused them? Use the MCP and state the age scope actually queried.

response.answer:
**Age scope queried:** FAERS reports for ages coded in **months 0 through 12**; records using other age units were excluded. This was a queried report subset, not all infants. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

### What the reports can tell a researcher

They show reaction terms and reporting counts recorded in that queried subset. Examples included vomiting (**117** reports), pyrexia (**98**), rash (**60**), irritability (**42**), seizure (**35**), acute hepatic failure (**28**), and liver injury (**28**). These are spontaneous-report terms; the returned population context for each term was **not established** beyond the search filter. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

### What they cannot establish

- **How often side effects occur:** The returned counts are reporting volume, not incidence or risk. No exposure denominator was available, so incidence or individual risk cannot be calculated. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)
- **Whether acetaminophen caused an event:** The reports do not establish causation. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)
- **Whether the findings apply to all infants or all exposed infants:** The queried results cannot be generalized to either group. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)
- **That each listed term is a confirmed adverse effect:** The extract does not establish that. No safety verdict should be inferred from these results, including from terms not appearing in the returned list. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

The query was bounded to the returned report subset; it was not an exhaustive assessment of all evidence. The MCP also states that the generated answer is not clinically validated. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

[S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)\\n- In seven infants aged four weeks, no adverse effects were reported. request.question: Using the parent medication information tool, summarize the sertraline evidence from LactMed and the product label. Separate measured milk exposure from observed infant outcomes. Include links and questions to ask a clinician. Do not give dosing or medication decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during breastfeeding

### Measured exposure

LactMed reports these **measured breast-milk concentrations**:

- In a pooled analysis of 15 mothers: sertraline averaged **45 mcg/L** (range **7–207 mcg/L**). [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)
- In 26 women sampled extensively over 24 hours: milk sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- At 2 months postpartum, four mothers had average milk concentrations of **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; samples were collected at random times. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline across three samples collected at random times. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- At four weeks postpartum, foremilk and hindmilk concentrations were **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively, in samples collected 13 hours after maternal administration. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In first-week postpartum trough samples from nine women, sertraline was **<5 mcg/L** in one woman and **11.1–24.5 mcg/L** in eight others. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In six women providing random milk samples, the median sertraline concentration was **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**); LactMed notes that sampling-time differences might affect these values. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In 15 mothers whose milk was sampled at predefined times over two days, the average concentration was **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**). [S42](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38841362/)

The returned LactMed extract did not include a complete infant-level concentration passage. It states that sertraline is usually not detected in infant serum and that norsertraline may be detectable at low levels in infant serum, but infant-level details are incomplete in the returned extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

The returned LactMed extract is truncated; its study count is not established from the extract.

- One 4-month-old infant had benign sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of 26 infants, no detectable acute adverse reactions were observed. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- In 14 mother–infant pairs, infant whole-blood serotonin levels were measured before and after maternal treatment; the extract reports no infant adverse effects in that study. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)
- In a study of 25 infants, six-month weight gain was reported as normal according to national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)
- In six infants aged 5–34 weeks, no clinical adverse reactions were noted at the time of the study. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)
- In seven infants aged four weeks, no adverse effects were reported. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367055/)
- A small study reported blunted pain responses among infants exposed to an SSRI prenatally and/or through breast milk; four of the 30 infants were exposed to sertraline. The comparison group consisted of unexposed infants of nondepressed mothers, so the extract does not establish the contribution of maternal depression or maternal behavior. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)
- **Separate case report:** a preterm infant born at 33 weeks developed hyperthermia, abnormal muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying. The report also described infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite; the infant’s later genetic metabolic findings and the authors’ attribution are part of that case report, not evidence that the outcome occurs generally. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)

### Product-label evidence

The retrieved label is **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, effective November 5, 2026. The tool did not confirm that it matches the specific product or formulation being used. DailyMed’s retrieved lactation section states that published data show low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk. In a pooled analysis of 53 mother–infant pairs, exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels equal to **2%** of maternal serum levels, with a range of **0–15%**; no adverse reactions were observed in those infants. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The label states that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. This is a label evidence limitation, not an observed infant outcome. The retrieved label extract also omitted the warnings, warnings-and-precautions, boxed-warning, and drug-interaction sections; their absence from the extract does not establish that the topics are absent from the complete labeling. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Questions to ask a clinician or pharmacist

- Does this evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?
- How closely do the reported study populations match my infant’s age, health, feeding pattern, and prematurity status?
- Which findings are measured exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
- What remains uncertain because the LactMed outcome and drug-level sections were truncated?
- What maternal and infant outcomes should be considered together before making any treatment change?
- Which symptoms or changes would warrant professional assessment?

Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss any change with the prescribing clinician. This MCP-generated answer has not undergone clinical framing review and is not clinically validated.

[S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- A small prospective study of eight primiparous women taking different serotonin-reuptake inhibitors, including one taking sertraline, reported delayed lactogenesis compared with 423 mothers not taking an SRI. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The selected DailyMed label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and its metabolites in human milk and that it contains no data on effects on milk production. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- At two months postpartum: sertraline **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L** in milk samples collected at random times. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a report involving a preterm infant: milk sertraline and norsertraline concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively, at random sampling times. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- Foremilk and hindmilk collected 13 hours after a dose contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a separate group of 26 infants, the extract reports no detectable acute adverse reactions during the study. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- Another passage reports normal six-month weight gain in infants in a study of breastfeeding mothers taking antidepressants; the extract does not establish that all findings were sertraline-specific. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- A small study of infants exposed to an SSRI prenatally alone or prenatally and through breast milk reported blunted pain responses compared with unexposed infants. Four of 30 infants were exposed to sertraline; the passage states that the comparison lacked a group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- An uncontrolled survey of 930 mothers taking an antidepressant reported infant drug-discontinuation symptoms in about 10% of infants; the result was not specific to sertraline. The passage reports elevated infant serum concentrations and states that the authors attributed the symptoms to sertraline exposure and reduced metabolism. This is a single case report, not a population estimate. request.question: Prepare an evidence brief for sertraline during lactation using the medication evidence brief tool. Include questions to ask my clinician, source links, and missing evidence limitations. Do not provide medication decisions or doses.

response.answer:
## Evidence brief: sertraline during lactation

**Identity:** The tool matched **sertraline** exactly as a single ingredient. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed reports a small observation in which six patients reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; the administered amounts were not reported. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A small prospective study of eight primiparous women taking different serotonin-reuptake inhibitors, including one taking sertraline, reported delayed lactogenesis compared with 423 mothers not taking an SRI. The extract states that feeding difficulties after postpartum day 4 did not differ statistically. This was a mixed-SRI study, not a sertraline-only study. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and its metabolites in human milk and that it contains no data on effects on milk production. This is one selected product label, not all formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Measured exposure

Retrieved LactMed milk measurements included:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, in a pooled analysis. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study with extensive milk sampling: sertraline **129 mcg/L**, range **11–938 mcg/L**; norsertraline **258 mcg/L**, range **20–1498 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- At two months postpartum: sertraline **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L** in milk samples collected at random times. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a report involving a preterm infant: milk sertraline and norsertraline concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively, at random sampling times. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Foremilk and hindmilk collected 13 hours after a dose contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Other reported milk findings included **<5 mcg/L**, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** with a range of **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**, and **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12–288 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The returned LactMed extract did not include a complete infant-level concentration section; infant-level information is therefore incomplete in this retrieval. A PubMed abstract reported detectable sertraline in three nursing infants and detectable desmethylsertraline in six; the abstract described the specimen as **infant serum**. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

These are research measurements, not dosing instructions, and do not establish safety.

### Observed infant outcomes

- LactMed reports benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in one four-month-old infant and spontaneously resolving agitation in the same case passage. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a separate group of 26 infants, the extract reports no detectable acute adverse reactions during the study. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Another passage reports normal six-month weight gain in infants in a study of breastfeeding mothers taking antidepressants; the extract does not establish that all findings were sertraline-specific. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A small study of infants exposed to an SSRI prenatally alone or prenatally and through breast milk reported blunted pain responses compared with unexposed infants. Four of 30 infants were exposed to sertraline; the passage states that the comparison lacked a group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- An uncontrolled survey of 930 mothers taking an antidepressant reported infant drug-discontinuation symptoms in about 10% of infants; the result was not specific to sertraline. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A separate case report describes a preterm infant born at 33 weeks who developed hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation disorders, and high-pitched crying. The passage reports elevated infant serum concentrations and states that the authors attributed the symptoms to sertraline exposure and reduced metabolism. This is a single case report, not a population estimate. [S30](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)[S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The Effects in Breastfed Infants section was truncated in the returned LactMed extract, so additional outcome details may be missing.

### FAERS report context

The returned FAERS query covered reports matching generic-name sertraline, cohort **“any,”** and was not lactation- or infant-specific. Reported terms and counts were:

| Reported term | Count |
|---|---:|
| Nausea | 14,075 |
| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |
| Fatigue | 13,021 |
| Headache | 11,284 |
| Anxiety | 10,530 |
| Diarrhoea | 10,499 |
| Dizziness | 9,741 |
| Depression | 9,612 |

These counts represent reporting volume, not rates, confirmed clinical outcomes, or causation. The queried population is not established, and the results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)[S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Literature retrieval limitations

The bounded PubMed search returned 129 records and displayed five records. Abstract text was retrieved for three requested PMIDs:

- Abstract retrieved: **12452737**, **38811474**, **9286185**
- No abstract text returned: **38133585**, **32320387**
- Unreturned PMIDs: none
- Failed abstract lookups: none

Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. Titles alone were not used as outcome evidence. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)[S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12452737/)[S48](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38811474/)[S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)[S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)[S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)

### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist

- Does this evidence apply to my exact formulation and all active ingredients?
- How closely do the study populations match my infant’s age, feeding pattern, gestational age, and prematurity status?
- Which findings measure milk or infant exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
- Which uncertainties or missing evidence are most important for an individualized discussion?

Use the evidence brief tool.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Questions to ask your clinician\\n\\n### Applying the evidence\\n- Does the evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?\\n- How closely do the studies match my baby\u2019s age, feeding pattern, gestational age, and prematurity status?\\n- Which findings measured drug exposure, and which evaluated clinical outcomes?\\n- What important uncertainties remain before making a treatment decision?\\n\\n### Breastmilk and infant exposure\\n- How should the reported breastmilk concentrations be interpreted for my situation?\\n- Does infant-level information need to be considered separately from milk measurements?\\n- Are there circumstances in which infant testing would be clinically useful?\\n- How should the metabolite norsertraline be considered when discussing exposure?\\n\\n### Observed infant findings\\n- How should we interpret the isolated reports of agitation, sleep myoclonus, sedation, or symptoms in a preterm infant?\\n- Which findings were observed outcomes, rather than source recommendations or theoretical concerns?\\n- What does the evidence show about infant growth and longer-term development, and what remains unestablished?\\n- What signs in my infant should prompt a call to the pediatrician?\\n\\n### Lactation and maternal outcomes\\n- What evidence is specific to sertraline rather than antidepressants or SSRIs as a group?\\n- How should reports of reduced milk supply or delayed lactation be interpreted?\\n- How might the underlying condition and its treatment affect breastfeeding outcomes independently of sertraline?\\n\\n### Follow-up and treatment planning\\n- How should my clinical need for sertraline be weighed alongside the breastfeeding evidence?\\n- What follow-up would address both my health and my infant\u2019s health?\\n- If treatment changes are being considered, what clinician-supervised plan accounts for risks associated with changing treatment?\\n\\n## Measured exposure\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed extract reports these **research milk concentrations**, separately from infant outcomes:\\n\\n- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**; range **7\u2013207 mcg/L** in a pooled analysis.\\n- Sertraline: average **129 mcg/L**; range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**; norsertraline: average **258 mcg/L**; range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L** in a 24-hour sampling study.\\n- Sertraline: **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline: **29 mcg/L** at random sampling times in one report.\\n- In a report involving a preterm infant, breastmilk sertraline and norsertraline concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively.\\n- Foremilk and hindmilk sertraline concentrations were **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively, 13 hours after a dose.\\n- Other reported milk measurements included **<5 mcg/L**, **11.1\u201324.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** with a range of **3.6\u201335.7 mcg/L**, and **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12\u2013288 request.question: Please prepare questions for my clinician about the evidence for sertraline during breastfeeding. Use the evidence brief tool.

response.answer:
## Questions to ask your clinician

### Applying the evidence
- Does the evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?
- How closely do the studies match my baby’s age, feeding pattern, gestational age, and prematurity status?
- Which findings measured drug exposure, and which evaluated clinical outcomes?
- What important uncertainties remain before making a treatment decision?

### Breastmilk and infant exposure
- How should the reported breastmilk concentrations be interpreted for my situation?
- Does infant-level information need to be considered separately from milk measurements?
- Are there circumstances in which infant testing would be clinically useful?
- How should the metabolite norsertraline be considered when discussing exposure?

### Observed infant findings
- How should we interpret the isolated reports of agitation, sleep myoclonus, sedation, or symptoms in a preterm infant?
- Which findings were observed outcomes, rather than source recommendations or theoretical concerns?
- What does the evidence show about infant growth and longer-term development, and what remains unestablished?
- What signs in my infant should prompt a call to the pediatrician?

### Lactation and maternal outcomes
- What evidence is specific to sertraline rather than antidepressants or SSRIs as a group?
- How should reports of reduced milk supply or delayed lactation be interpreted?
- How might the underlying condition and its treatment affect breastfeeding outcomes independently of sertraline?

### Follow-up and treatment planning
- How should my clinical need for sertraline be weighed alongside the breastfeeding evidence?
- What follow-up would address both my health and my infant’s health?
- If treatment changes are being considered, what clinician-supervised plan accounts for risks associated with changing treatment?

## Measured exposure

The retrieved LactMed extract reports these **research milk concentrations**, separately from infant outcomes:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**; range **7–207 mcg/L** in a pooled analysis.
- Sertraline: average **129 mcg/L**; range **11–938 mcg/L**; norsertraline: average **258 mcg/L**; range **20–1,498 mcg/L** in a 24-hour sampling study.
- Sertraline: **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline: **29 mcg/L** at random sampling times in one report.
- In a report involving a preterm infant, breastmilk sertraline and norsertraline concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively.
- Foremilk and hindmilk sertraline concentrations were **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively, 13 hours after a dose.
- Other reported milk measurements included **<5 mcg/L**, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** with a range of **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**, and **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12–288 mcg/L**.

The returned LactMed exposure extract did **not** include a separate infant-level excerpt; therefore, infant-level availability is missing in that extract. These measurements do not establish safety or determine an individual treatment plan. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

## Retrieval limitations

- The LactMed “Drug Levels” and “Effects in Breastfed Infants” sections were truncated in the returned extract; the record should not be treated as complete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Abstract text was retrieved for 3 of 5 requested PubMed records. No abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**; this is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that those research records do not exist. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- The retrieved FAERS query returned reports including nausea (**14,075**), “drug ineffective” (**13,855**), fatigue (**13,021**), headache (**11,284**), anxiety (**10,530**), diarrhoea (**10,499**), dizziness (**9,741**), and depression (**9,612**). These are reporting volume from the queried report subset, not rates, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation; the queried population was not confirmed as lactating people or breastfed infants. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

[S15](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/2591497/properties.json)\\n\\nThe selected DailyMed label states that no human pregnancy data are available to evaluate risks of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. The label is for **QUVIVIQ (daridorexant) tablet, film coated**, Idorsia Pharmaceuticals Ltd.; the extract is one product label, not all formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef)\\n\\n| Evidence axis | Retrieved findings |\\n|---|---|\\n| **Effects on the pregnant person** | **Empty clinical-findings row:** no human maternal pregnancy outcomes were retrieved. In animal reproduction data, decreased maternal weight gain and food consumption were reported in pregnant rabbits. This is animal evidence, not an observed human pregnancy effect. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |\\n| **Measured fetal or infant exposure** | **Empty row:** no measured human fetal or infant exposure data were retrieved. No fetal, cord, or infant concentration measurements were reported in the retrieved material. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |\\n| **Observed fetal or infant outcomes** | **Empty human observed-outcome row:** no human fetal or infant outcome findings were retrieved. The label provides animal context: the described rat and rabbit studies did not report fetal toxicity or malformation, and the described rat gestation/lactation study did not report maternal or developmental toxicity. These were animal observations, not human pregnancy outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |\\n\\n### FAERS report-only context\\n\\nThe returned FAERS query covered reports matching the stated daridorexant and pregnancy-exposure terms; it was **not a complete exposed population**, and the source population was not established in the returned records. Reported terms and counts were: fetal exposure during pregnancy (11), premature baby (10), neonatal hypotonia (9), moaning (9), neonatal behavioural syndrome (9), neonatal respiratory distress (9), cardiac disorder (7), and cardiomegaly (7). These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; they do not establish causation, and no exposure denominator was available. The results cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22daridorexant%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S11](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)\\n\\n### Maternal pharmacokinetic data\\n\\n**No maternal pharmacokinetic data were retrieved** from the label\u2019s Clinical Considerations section or the curated PubMed pharmacokinetic search. The pharmacokinetic query returned no records. This is a retrieval finding, not evidence of safety. ## Pregnancy evidence brief: daridorexant

[S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef)

[S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |
| **Measured fetal or infant exposure** | **Empty row:** no measured human fetal or infant exposure data were retrieved. No fetal, cord, or infant concentration measurements were reported in the retrieved material. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |
| **Observed fetal or infant outcomes** | **Empty human observed-outcome row:** no human fetal or infant outcome findings were retrieved. The label provides animal context: the described rat and rabbit studies did not report fetal toxicity or malformation, and the described rat gestation/lactation study did not report maternal or developmental toxicity. These were animal observations, not human pregnancy outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |

### FAERS report-only context

The returned FAERS query covered reports matching the stated daridorexant and pregnancy-exposure terms; it was **not a complete exposed population**, and the source population was not established in the returned records. Reported terms and counts were: fetal exposure during pregnancy (11), premature baby (10), neonatal hypotonia (9), moaning (9), neonatal behavioural syndrome (9), neonatal respiratory distress (9), cardiac disorder (7), and cardiomegaly (7). These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; they do not establish causation, and no exposure denominator was available. The results cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22daridorexant%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S11](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

- “Drugs for chronic insomnia.” [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630579/)

## Pregnancy evidence brief: lamotrigine

**Identity:** The retrieved record matched lamotrigine exactly. The search concerned the single ingredient, not combination-product safety.[S27](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)

### Effects on the pregnant person

**Lamotrigine-specific maternal clinical effects:** No lamotrigine-specific maternal adverse-outcome finding was retrieved in the evidence extract. This is a retrieval gap, not evidence that no maternal effects exist.

The selected DailyMed record describes epilepsy-associated pregnancy risks, including preeclampsia, preterm labor, hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. That passage presents underlying-disease context and does not establish that lamotrigine caused those outcomes.[S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The selected product label was **“LAMOTRIGINE KIT … [OWP Pharmaceuticals, Inc.]”**, with an effective date of **October 12, 2026**. The extracted adult adverse-reaction, warnings, and warnings-and-precautions sections were missing; the pregnancy section was truncated in the general section extract. Missing sections do not establish absence of information.[S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Fetal exposure

The label states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It reports decreased lamotrigine concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery.[S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The retrieved maternal-pharmacokinetic material did not provide numeric human maternal concentration, clearance, or exposure results specific to lamotrigine. A retrieved PubMed abstract describes concentration measurements in serum and breast milk in a naturalistic sample of 60 mothers and reports a high concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine in breast milk. This is lactation exposure information, not a measured fetal concentration, and the abstract does not provide a lamotrigine-specific participant count.[S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

A recruiting study, **NCT05450978**, is described as examining antiseizure-medication clearance, physiological factors affecting blood concentrations, and exposure to unborn children in pregnant adults with epilepsy. It has no posted results in the returned record; the study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability.[S9](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05450978)

**Retrieved gap:** No verified numeric fetal lamotrigine concentration or human placental-transfer measurement was returned.

### Fetal and infant outcomes

#### Major congenital malformations

The selected label reports the following registry findings for **first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy**:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: **2.2%** among **1,558 infants**, with 95% CI 1.6%–3.1%.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: **2.0%** among **1,562 infants**.
- EURAP: **2.9%** among **2,514 exposures**, with 95% CI 2.3%–3.7%.

The label states that frequencies were similar to general-population estimates, while noting that outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit interpretation.[S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

#### Oral clefts

The NAAED Pregnancy Registry reported isolated oral clefts at **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200 infants exposed early in pregnancy**, described in the label as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. The label states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control study reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**, with 95% CI 0.8–2.63.[S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The completed EUROCAT registry study record states that its case-control study found no statistically significant increased risk of oral clefts compared with other defects after in-utero lamotrigine exposure. Its primary comparison group consisted of malformed infants without oral clefts; the record states that the registers did not collect data on non-malformed infants.[S4](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01055327)

#### Other fetal and infant outcomes

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It reports that the extracted evidence did not suggest increased risk with lamotrigine monotherapy, but also states that differences in outcome definition, ascertainment, and comparator groups limit conclusions.[S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A 2023 naturalistic study of 60 mothers reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborns and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The abstract covers multiple psychotropic medicines and does not establish lamotrigine-specific sample size or lamotrigine-only outcome estimates.[S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### FAERS report-only context

For the returned query of lamotrigine reports containing the reaction term “foetal exposure during pregnancy,” FAERS reporting counts included:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Foetal exposure during pregnancy | 3,527 |
| Atrial septal defect | 357 |
| Congenital anomaly | 327 |
| Premature baby | 257 |
| Ventricular septal defect | 205 |
| Patent ductus arteriosus | 153 |
| Spina bifida | 143 |
| Hypospadias | 135 |

These are reporting volumes for reports matching the stated query, not confirmed clinical outcomes, incidence rates, or proof of causation. Exposure denominators were unavailable, and the returned source population was not established. The results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to lamotrigine.[S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)[S14](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

- The PubMed search was bounded and not a systematic review.[S11](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)[S12](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29+AND+%28%22Pharmacokinetics%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Drug+Elimination+Routes%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pharmacokinetic%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+clearance%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22area+under+the+curve%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22dose+adjustment%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=3&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

- Lamotrigine-specific maternal clinical-outcome evidence was not retrieved in the evidence extract.

### Questions for a clinician

1. Which of these findings apply to my indication, formulation, co-medications, and whether lamotrigine is used alone or with other medicines?

No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Sertraline during lactation: research summary\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed record reports these **milk concentrations**:\\n\\n- Pooled analysis of 15 mothers: mean sertraline **45 mcg/L**; range **7\u2013207 mcg/L**. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)\\n- Study of 26 women, about 5\u201336 weeks postpartum, with 24-hour milk and serum sampling: mean milk sertraline **129 mcg/L**; range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**; mean norsertraline **258 mcg/L**; range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)\\n- Four mothers at two months postpartum: mean milk sertraline **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L**, sampled at random times. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In one report involving a preterm infant, milk levels averaged **201 mcg/L for sertraline** and **358 mcg/L for norsertraline** on three randomly timed days. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)\\n- In one mother, foremilk and hindmilk collected 13 hours after exposure contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a first-week-postpartum sampling study, sertraline was **<5 mcg/L** in one woman; levels in the other eight women ranged from **11.1\u201324.5 mcg/L**. The record notes that timing may affect those values. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In six women providing random milk samples, the median sertraline concentration was **11.3 mcg/L**, range **3.6\u201335.7 mcg/L**; the record notes that the sampling timing may make these values inaccurate. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In 15 mothers providing samples at prespecified times, mean milk concentration was **87 mcg/L**, range **12\u2013288 mcg/L**. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed extract does **not** include the infant-level concentration passage in full. Its summary states that sertraline is usually not detected in infant serum and that norsertraline is often detectable in low levels in infant serum; the exact infant-level data should therefore be checked in the complete record. Milk concentration is an exposure measurement, not an infant clinical outcome and does not establish safety. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\nReported findings were mixed and came from small studies, surveys, and case reports:\\n\\n- One 4-month-old infant had benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a study of 26 infants, no acute adverse reactions were detected. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)\\n- In a study of 14 mother\u2013infant pairs, infant whole-blood serotonin measurements were reported before and after maternal treatment, and no infant adverse effects were reported. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)\\n- In a report of 25 infants followed through six months, reported weight gain was within national growth standards and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)\\n- No clinical adverse reactions were noted at the time of study in six infants aged 5\u201334 weeks; another report described no adverse effects in seven 4-week-old infants. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)\\n- A study of infants exposed to an SSRI before birth and through breastfeeding reported blunted pain responses compared with infants of nondepressed, unexposed mothers. Four of the 30 exposed infants received sertraline. The returned passage states that the study lacked a comparison group of depressed mothers not taking medication, so an effect related to maternal depression or behavior could not be separated from medication exposure. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)\\n- An uncontrolled online survey of 930 breastfeeding mothers taking antidepressants reported infant discontinuation symptoms in about 10% of infants. The survey included different antidepressants and combined pregnancy and lactation exposure, so the returned record does not provide a sertraline-specific estimate. [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20807106/)\\n- One mother reported sedation in her infant while taking sertraline with other medicines, including a benzodiazepine and a sedative-hypnotic; the co-exposures mean this report does not isolate sertraline. [S25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22504099/)\\n\\n**Separate preterm-infant case report:** A preterm infant born at 33 weeks developed hyperthermia, altered muscle tone, and high-pitched crying during the reported exposure period. The report states that infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite were measured, and that symptoms later dissipated after breastfeeding was discontinued while serum levels decreased. The report attributed the episode to serotonergic overstimulation in the setting of reduced metabolism, but this is a single case report involving prematurity and cannot establish frequency or applicability to other infants. The returned LactMed section is truncated after the beginning of another case, so later details are missing. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)[S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Lactation and milk-production findings\\n\\nThese findings concern the lactating person or breastfeeding behavior, not measured infant exposure:\\n\\n- A midwife described six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; this was an uncontrolled observation, and maternal treatment details were not fully reported. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- A small prospective study of eight mothers taking serotonin reuptake inhibitors\u2014including one taking sertraline\u2014reported delayed onset of milk secretory activation compared with 423 mothers not taking an SRI. Because several medicines were represented and only one participant took sertraline, the result does not establish a sertraline-specific effect. [S20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19965920/)\\n- Observational studies involving antidepressants or SSRIs reported differences in breastfeeding initiation, continuation, or discharge rates.
